children: U.S. stocks recouped some of their recent losses as oil prices stabilized and confidence grew in the Federal Reserve's ability to contain inflation.

The Dow Jones Industrial Average rose 316.14 points, or 0.61%, to 51778.04. The S&P 500 gained 85.95 points, or 1.14%, to 7637.76 and the tech-heavy Nasdaq Composite added 439.87 points, or 1.69%, to 26418.30.

Comfort with Fed Chairman Kevin Warsh's strategy and hopes for a rapid return of Saudi oil to market tamed inflation concerns and crude futures. Oil futures declined 52 cents to $101.91 a barrel. Still, the risk of energy inflation loomed large as a prominent commodities strategist at JPMorgan warned it was becoming increasingly difficult to predict the course of the Middle East war and its effect on oil prices.

The yield on the two-year Treasury declined 0.038 percentage point to 4.688%. The yield on the 10-year note fell 0.057 percentage point to 4.946% from a 19-year high. The yield on the 30-year bond fell 0.050 percentage point to 5.296%.
The U.S. dollar was more or less flat as traders' inflation nerves were eased by the Fed policy statement and oil's slippage.
Gold futures rose $13.90, or 0.3%, to $4360.20 a troy ounce.

Housing starts fell 2.6% in August to 1.275 million, contrary to expectations for an increase. The property market remains the soft underbelly of the U.S. economy, and the housing-start data echoed weakness in home-builder confidence earlier in the week. Pending home sales rose slightly in August from July levels, but still dropped from the 2025 tally.
New weekly jobless claims fell by 10,000 to 196,000 in the latest tally.

Shares of private-equity firms rose slightly but remained under pressure as executives warned that higher interest rates may perpetuate a phenomenon of "zombie funds." When companies purchased via buyout funds cannot be sold on, investor capital languishes in such funds for years. Shares of Blackstone rose 1.6% to $125.41, but are 19% lower this year. Apollo Global shares added 1.2% to $126, but are down by 13% in 2026.

Volvo Car, the Swedish car maker majority owned by Chinese firm Zhejiang Geely Holding, said it would launch 13 new car models by the end of the decade in an effort to rekindle consumer demand for the struggling brand. Volvo also acknowledged that its electric-vehicle strategy in the U.S. was in need of revision, with plug-in hybrids now viewed as a "stepping stone."

Mastercard launched an artificial-intelligence payment option for everyday purchases, partnering with the startup Alchemy to allow consumers to set up AI agents for online shopping. Shares ticked down 0.4% to $565.73.

Shares of Ultragenyx Pharmaceutical rose 13% to $14.50 after the Food and Drug Administration granted commercial approval to the biotech firm's gene therapy for pediatric patients with a rare neurodevelopmental disease.
